title: Decision Boundary Design
summary: Decision boundary design determines which decision points in an AI-assisted product may be handled autonomously, which require human confirmation, and which require independent human judgement. The practice covers boundary identification, boundary calibration and boundary implementation.
keyFacts: Decision boundary design applies to decision points where a system makes a choice, executes an action or provides a recommendation that shapes later events.
The practice distinguishes autonomous AI action, human confirmation and independent human judgement.
Boundary identification determines which decision points belong in each category.
Boundary calibration sets consequence and confidence thresholds as design decisions rather than only technical parameters.
Boundary implementation designs the interactions that enforce the selected boundary at the moment of decision.
A technically present override is not a meaningful boundary if it is cognitively expensive to use.
The Puraite AI systematic review example used blinded mode to enforce human independent judgement before AI recommendation exposure.
The Callsign fraud detection example separated model scores, policy thresholds and human policy configuration.
The non-model examples are not AI-governance instances; their uncertainty concerns sources, links, protocols and clocks rather than model confidence.

bodySections.heading: Decision Boundary Design in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies decision boundary design as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Decision Boundary Design Allocates Consequential Decisions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Decision boundary design is the practice of determining which decision points an AI system decides autonomously, which require human confirmation, and which require human judgement independent of the AI recommendation, then designing interactions that enforce those distinctions.

Decision boundary design applies where a system makes a choice, executes an action, or provides a recommendation that will shape later events. It is not limited to adding an override control. The practice identifies the decision boundary, calibrates the threshold for crossing it, and implements the interaction that enforces it.

In products with no model, the equivalent design problem is the allocation between a touchscreen and a physical control, and between what an interface may assert and what the system beneath it can evidence. Those examples are not AI examples; their uncertainty concerns sources, links, protocols, and clocks rather than model confidence.

bodySections.heading: Autonomous AI Action, Human Confirmation, and Independent Human Judgement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Decision boundary design determines which decision points are appropriate for autonomous AI action, which require human confirmation, and which require independent human judgement. The practice treats this allocation as a design and governance problem, not only as a technical configuration problem.

Autonomous AI action is appropriate when the consequence of error is low and reversible, AI confidence is high, and the volume of decisions makes human review impractical. Human confirmation is appropriate when the consequence is moderate or the action is irreversible. Independent human judgement is appropriate when consequence is high, governance requires epistemic independence, or AI data coverage is insufficient for the specific decision context.

Decision boundary design also determines how the interface records the difference between an AI recommendation and a human decision. A record that does not distinguish recommendation from decision weakens the boundary because it obscures who or what made the consequential choice.

bodySections.heading: Boundary Identification, Calibration, and Implementation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Decision boundary design has three separate activities: boundary identification, boundary calibration, and boundary implementation. Each activity answers a different question about the same decision point.

Boundary identification determines which decision points belong in each category. It asks whether the AI may act autonomously, whether a human must confirm the action, or whether the human must make an independent judgement with the AI as reference rather than recommendation.

Boundary calibration sets thresholds. It asks at what consequence level autonomous AI action becomes inappropriate, and at what AI confidence level recommendation becomes inappropriate without disclosure. These thresholds are design decisions informed by consequence analysis, governance requirements, and operational context; they are not only technical parameters.

Boundary implementation designs the enforcing interaction. It specifies what happens at a consequential decision point, how confirmation is structured, how AI confidence is communicated at the moment of decision, and how the interface distinguishes between the AI recommendation and the human decision in the record.

bodySections.heading: A Meaningful Override Must Be Usable at the Moment of Decision
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Decision boundary design treats human override as an interaction design problem. A boundary can be technically present but not meaningful if it is cognitively expensive to cross, such as when the override is buried, dismissal requires multiple steps, or the interface offers no support for the override decision.

The risk is default acceptance. Users may accept AI recommendations not because they agree with them, but because the path of least resistance leads to acceptance.

The interaction must make the boundary legible. Users should understand when they are acting on AI output and when they are acting on their own judgement. The friction must also be calibrated to the consequence of the decision rather than applied uniformly.

Uniform friction can train users to click through. Friction at consequential decision points protects the decisions that need protection without impeding decisions that do not need the same protection.

bodySections.heading: When Creative Navy Applies Decision Boundary Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy applies decision boundary design after trust-and-oversight analysis and behavioural requirements definition have identified where boundaries are needed and why. At that point, decision boundary design specifies how the required boundaries are implemented in interaction behaviour.

Decision boundary design is also used during Concept Convergence when evaluating AI interaction patterns. Different design directions often contain implicit boundary positions, and making those positions explicit is necessary for comparing them.

In enterprise and regulated contexts, decision boundary design is used before governance review. The boundary map becomes part of the evidence that the product's human oversight structure is meaningful rather than nominal.

bodySections.heading: AI Case Examples of Decision Boundary Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Puraite AI systematic review case, the decision boundary was methodologically defined. Inclusion and exclusion decisions had to be made by human reviewers exercising independent judgement. Blinded mode enforced the epistemic independence boundary by withholding the AI recommendation until after the human reviewer made an assessment. Confidence display at decision points implemented calibration, and override parity meant the override interaction required no more cognitive effort than acceptance.

In the Callsign fraud detection case, the decision boundary separated what the model decided, what policy decided, and what the human decided. The model produced risk scores. The policy layer determined thresholds and workflow triggers. Human analysts configured policies and strategic exceptions. Policy evaluation mode separated read-only analysis from configuration, and high-consequence policy changes affecting live transaction volumes above specified thresholds were flagged when modified.

In the Owkin K biomedical AI case, the decision boundary separated what K knows from what the researcher decides to act on. K's responses were bounded by dataset scope, and that scope was made visible through data-source display and scope-edge flagging. Query framing was also treated as a decision point so that researchers framed their query with knowledge of K's capability scope before committing to a question.

In the Hudex intelligence analysis case, the boundary between AI-generated summary and expert analytical engagement was implemented through progressive disclosure. The project overview showed AI-generated high-level analysis, and the researcher decided whether to engage with detailed AI clustering. Within the dondogram, the depth of AI analysis visible was controlled by user action rather than displayed by default.

bodySections.heading: Non-Model Boundary Examples Are Not AI-Governance Evidence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Four non-model engagements show the same practice allocating boundaries between what an interface may assert and what the system beneath it can evidence. These engagements are not AI work and should not be treated as AI-governance examples. Their uncertainty is a property of sources, links, protocols, and clocks, not of model confidence.

In KISPE Space, the product boundary excluded autonomous operational decisions, inferred adversary classification or targeting, guaranteed service-quality prediction, and substitution for existing command systems. The enforcing behavioural rule was that system errors never invent operational conclusions. A transport or access failure is reported as a transport or access failure, with what is still known from cache, and is not translated into a statement about adversaries, sensors, or service status.

In Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF work, send eligibility was a derived boundary. Whether a digital call could be transmitted was computed from recipient identity validity, record freshness, channel lawfulness under the active regional profile, and station readiness. The computation was repeated at the moment of sending, so a recipient could not drift during preparation. A visible vessel was not necessarily a callable vessel when it lacked a usable registered identity.

In Schone Airspace Group uncrewed aircraft Mission Control, command eligibility was a derived boundary. Whether an action could be offered was computed from source freshness, link condition, and channel permission, not from selection alone. Where link condition and sample freshness could not establish eligibility, availability was shown as unknown rather than ready.

In the European manufacturer engagement for uncrewed systems and tactical command-and-control software, the radial menu was made non-contextual because the system could not reliably determine whether a vehicle was airborne or on the ground. The design showed every option rather than asserting a distinction the system beneath it could not evidence. This was a boundary about system knowledge, not model confidence.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Decision Boundary Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Decision boundary design produces a boundary map. The boundary map identifies decision points, assigns each decision point to autonomous action, human confirmation, or independent human judgement, and records the reason for that assignment.

Decision boundary design also produces interaction rules. These rules specify how the interface handles the decision point, how friction is introduced or avoided, how confidence or data scope is shown, and how the record separates AI recommendation from human decision.

In enterprise and regulated contexts, the boundary map can form part of governance evidence. Its purpose is to show that human oversight is meaningful in the interaction design, rather than only nominal in policy language.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Limits of the Practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Decision boundary design does not guarantee that a human will make the correct decision. It specifies where human judgement, confirmation, or autonomous action belongs, and designs the interaction that enforces that allocation.

Decision boundary design also does not convert non-model systems into AI systems. In non-model examples, the relevant boundary is between what the interface may assert and what the underlying system can evidence. Those examples should not be read as claims about model inference, AI confidence, or AI governance.

The available engagement evidence describes boundary structures and design decisions. It does not establish that any boundary prevented an error or incident.

strongClaims: Decision boundary design allocates decision points between autonomous AI action, human confirmation and independent human judgment, then designs interactions to enforce those distinctions.
Boundary calibration sets consequence and AI-confidence thresholds as design decisions informed by consequence analysis, governance requirements and operational context.
A technically present override is not necessarily a meaningful decision boundary if it is cognitively expensive to cross.
In the Puraite AI systematic review case, blinded mode enforced independent human judgment by withholding the AI recommendation until after the human assessment.
In the Callsign fraud detection case, model outputs, policy consequences and human policy configuration were separated as decision boundaries.
In the Owkin K biomedical AI case, dataset-scope visibility was used as a decision boundary between what K knows and what researchers decide to act on.
The KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group and European manufacturer examples are non-model boundary examples and are not AI-governance instances.

Decision boundary design is used after trust-and-oversight analysis and behavioural requirements definition, during Concept Convergence, and before governance review in enterprise and regulated contexts.
limitations: The practice does not establish that a boundary prevented an error or incident; the available evidence describes design decisions and boundary structures.
The KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group and European manufacturer examples are non-model examples and must not be treated as AI-governance instances.
No safety, certification, type-approval, weapons-review or regulatory credential is established for the non-model examples.
The source provides sequence and practice use, but no engagement dates.
The page does not claim shipped-as-designed or design-fidelity outcomes for KISPE Space, Raymarine or the European manufacturer engagement.
